provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the main topics covered in SSS two Physics.
The students should be able to solve basic mechanics problems.

Introduction:
Last term we covered fundamental physics concepts. Today we will revise these topics to prepare for new material.

Content:
We will review mechanics including forces, motion, and energy. Waves properties and sound will also be covered. Students should remember Newton's laws of motion and how they apply to everyday situations like a danfo bus accelerating or braking. We will work through examples of wave calculations including frequency and wavelength.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past WAEC mechanics questions and present their solutions to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. State Newton's second law of motion.
2. Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 1000kg car at 2m/s².
3. Explain how the concept of wave motion applies to both sound and light.
4. A wave has a frequency of 50Hz. What is its period?

Summary:
Today's revision covered key SSS two physics topics needed as foundation for this term's work.

topics.title: Measurement and units
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between fundamental and derived quantities.
The students should be able to calculate percentage error in measurements.

Introduction:
In physics, accurate measurement is essential. We build on your knowledge of units from previous years.

Content:
Fundamental quantities include length, mass, time, and electric current. Derived quantities are combinations like speed (m/s) or force (kgm/s²). The dimension of a quantity shows its relation to fundamental quantities. When measuring the length of a desk with a metre rule, errors can occur due to parallax or instrument limitations. Percentage error is calculated as (error/true value) × 100%. For example, if a student measures a 1.00m table as 1.02m, the percentage error is 2%.

Class activity:
Students will measure the dimensions of their textbooks using different instruments and calculate the percentage error for each measurement.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three fundamental physical quantities.
2. Differentiate between precision and accuracy.
3. Calculate the percentage error if a student measures 9.8m/s² as 10.0m/s².
4. What is the dimension of work?

Summary:
Understanding measurement and error analysis is crucial for physics experiments and calculations.

topics.title: Kinematics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to interpret motion graphs.
The students should be able to apply equations of motion to solve problems.

Introduction:
We studied motion in SSS two. Today we will deepen our understanding with graphs and equations.

Content:
Kinematics describes motion without considering forces. Distance is total path length while displacement is straight-line change in position. Speed is distance/time while velocity is displacement/time. Motion graphs include position-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs. The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement. The equations of motion are: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as. For example, if a danfo bus accelerates from rest at 2m/s² for 10s, its final velocity is 20m/s and distance covered is 100m.

Class activity:
Students will create position-time and velocity-time graphs for different motion scenarios and solve related problems.

Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between speed and velocity.
2. A car accelerates uniformly from 10m/s to 30m/s in 5s. Calculate its acceleration.
3. Sketch a velocity-time graph for an object moving with constant velocity.
4. What does the slope of a position-time graph represent?

Summary:
Kinematics provides the mathematical framework for describing motion in various situations.

topics.title: Dynamics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state and apply Newton's laws of motion.
The students should be able to solve problems involving momentum and impulse.

Introduction:
Last week we studied motion without considering causes. Today we examine forces that cause motion.

Content:
Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net force. Newton's second law states that F = ma. Newton's third law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Momentum is mass times velocity (p = mv). Impulse is force times time and equals change in momentum. When a kerosene stove falls from a table, gravity applies a force causing acceleration. The impulse when it hits the ground depends on the force and time of impact.

Class activity:
Students will conduct an experiment using trolleys and weights to demonstrate Newton's laws and conservation of momentum.

Evaluation questions:
1. State Newton's third law of motion and give an example.
2. Calculate the momentum of a 1000kg car moving at 20m/s.
3. A 0.05kg bullet fired from a gun with a velocity of 300m/s. What is the recoil velocity of the gun if its mass is 2kg?
4. Differentiate between elastic and inelastic collisions.

Summary:
Dynamics explains how forces affect motion and introduces the important concept of momentum.

topics.title: Work, energy, power
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define work, energy, and power and their units.
The students should be able to solve conservation of energy problems.

Introduction:
Energy is essential for all processes. We build on your understanding of these concepts from previous classes.

Content:
Work is done when a force causes displacement (W = Fd cos θ). Energy is the capacity to do work. Power is the rate of doing work (P = W/t). Units are joule for work and energy, watt for power. Potential energy is stored energy (mgh for gravitational). Kinetic energy is energy of motion (½mv²). Energy conservation states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. When lifting a bucket of water from a well, work is done against gravity, increasing potential energy. When released, this converts to kinetic energy.

Class activity:
Students will calculate the work done and power required to climb different flights of stairs in the school.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define work and state its SI unit.
2. A man pushes a wheelbarrow with 50N force over 10m. Calculate the work done.
3. Differentiate between potential and kinetic energy.
4. A 2kg ball falls from 5m height. Calculate its kinetic energy just before hitting the ground.

Summary:
Work, energy, and power are fundamental concepts that explain many physical phenomena in our daily lives.

topics.title: Circular motion
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define angular velocity and centripetal acceleration.
The students should be able to solve problems involving circular motion.

Introduction:
We have studied linear motion. Many objects move in circular paths, like vehicles roundabouts.

Content:
In circular motion, objects move in a circle at constant speed but changing velocity direction. Angular velocity (ω) is angle turned per unit time (ω = θ/t). Centripetal acceleration (a) is v²/r or ω²r, directed toward center. Centripetal force (F) is mv²/r or mω²r. For example, a car going round a curve experiences centripetal force provided by friction between tires and road. If friction is insufficient, the car skids outward. In Nigeria, during harmattan season, reduced friction on dusty roads increases the risk of skidding in circular motion.

Class activity:
Students will whirl a bucket of water in vertical circles to observe centripetal force and calculate minimum speed to keep water in the bucket.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define angular velocity and state its unit.
2. A car goes round a circular track of radius 50m at 10m/s. Calculate its centripetal acceleration.
3. Differentiate between centripetal and centrifugal force.
4. Explain why passengers feel pushed outward when a vehicle turns a corner.

Summary:
Circular motion involves special considerations due to continuously changing direction of velocity.

topics.title: Waves: properties
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define wave terms and interpret wave equations.
The students should be able to sketch and interpret wave graphs.

Introduction:
We have studied motion in straight lines. Waves transfer energy without matter transfer.

Content:
Waves are disturbances that transfer energy. Transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to direction (light waves). Longitudinal waves have oscillations parallel to direction (sound waves). Wave properties include amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and period. Wave equation is v = fλ. Wave graphs show displacement against position or time. For example, when a market trader strikes a metal pot, sound waves travel through air to reach customers. The amplitude determines loudness while frequency determines pitch.

Class activity:
Students will create transverse and longitudinal wave models using ropes and slinkies and measure their properties.

Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between transverse and longitudinal waves.
2. State the wave equation and define each term.
3. A wave has frequency 200Hz and speed 340m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
4. Sketch a displacement-position graph for a transverse wave.

Summary:
Waves have unique properties that distinguish them from other forms of energy transfer.

topics.title: Sound
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain resonance and harmonics in sound.
The students should be able to solve problems involving sound waves.

Introduction:
Sound is important in our daily communication. We will examine its special properties.

Content:
Sound is a longitudinal wave that requires medium for propagation. Speed of sound in air is about 340m/s. Resonance occurs when frequency matches natural frequency, causing large amplitude vibrations. Harmonics are integer multiples of fundamental frequency. When a musician plays a local drum, different harmonics create the rich sound quality. In pipes, closed ends have displacement nodes while open ends have antinodes. For example, when water is added to a bottle and blown across the top, different notes are produced as the air column length changes.

Class activity:
Students will use resonance tubes to determine the speed of sound and investigate harmonics in open and closed pipes.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain resonance and give an example.
2. Differentiate between fundamental frequency and harmonics.
3. Calculate the frequency of the third harmonic in a 1m long open pipe.
4. Why does sound travel faster in solids than in air?

Summary:
Sound waves have unique properties that allow for music communication and various applications in technology.

topics.title: Light: reflection and refraction
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the laws of reflection and refraction.
The students should be able to draw ray diagrams for mirrors and lenses.

Introduction:
Light enables us to see the world. Today we examine how light behaves when it meets surfaces.

Content:
Reflection is bouncing of light from a surface. Laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; incident ray, reflected ray, and normal are coplanar. Refraction is bending of light when entering different medium. Laws of refraction: incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar; ratio of sines is constant (n = sin i/sin r). Plane mirrors produce virtual images same size as object. Convex lenses converge light while concave lenses diverge light. When sunlight passes through a window, it refracts at the air-glass interface, causing the beam to bend.

Class activity:
Students will use ray boxes and optical benches to investigate reflection and refraction, and construct ray diagrams for different mirror and lens configurations.

Evaluation questions:
1. State the laws of reflection.
2. Differentiate between real and virtual images.
3. Calculate the refractive index if light enters water from air at 30° and refracts to 22°.
4. Sketch a ray diagram showing image formation by a convex lens.

Summary:
Light reflection and refraction explain many optical phenomena and are fundamental to understanding mirrors and lenses.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply knowledge from all topics to solve exam questions.
The students should be able to identify question patterns in WAEC physics.

Introduction:
We have covered many topics this term. Today we practice applying this knowledge to exam questions.

Content:
We will review key concepts from measurement, kinematics, dynamics, work energy power, circular motion, waves, sound, and light. Students should focus on problem-solving techniques and unit conversions. Common question patterns include calculations involving Newton's laws, energy conservation, wave properties, and optical instruments. For example, WAEC often asks questions combining kinematics with dynamics, or wave calculations with practical applications. Students should practice showing all working and including units in answers.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to solve selected WAEC past questions and present their solutions to the class with explanations.

Evaluation questions:
1. A car of mass 1200kg accelerates from rest at 2m/s². Calculate its kinetic energy after 5s.
2. Explain the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves with examples.
3. Calculate the frequency of a wave if its wavelength is 0.5m and speed is 300m/s.
4. A convex lens has focal length 15cm. An object 5cm high is placed 25cm from the lens. Calculate image distance and height.

Summary:
Regular practice of past questions helps students become familiar with exam patterns and improve problem-solving skills.
